prompt.context: Our client is a large national health care payer (health insurance company, think Aetna) exploring the launch of a new disease management ("DM") program to better serve its 5 million members. The idea is to hire and train a team of "Health Coaches" to specialize in a single disease area (e.g., heart disease, diabetes, etc.). Each Coach will manage a portfolio of patients to reduce the costs of overall health expenditures (e.g., reminders to take drugs, provide limited medical advice, suggested diet, etc.). Studies show that once-a-month contact with each patient reduces health spending by 5%, on average.
prompt.question: Should our client launch the program? If so, what steps should it take?

clarifying_info.q: What are the competitive dynamics in this space?
clarifying_info.a: With spiraling health care costs, the industry is under pressure to innovate. Assume our client is first to market. Past attempts to purely automate disease management have yielded minimal savings.
All activity is conducted remotely via phone/email. A typical profile is a registered nurse who wants to work from home.

clarifying_info.q: How many members can a Health Coach contact?
clarifying_info.a: It is difficult to actually reach patients, so Coaches can contact 8 members per day. Assume 25 working days per month.

clarifying_info.q: What does it cost to employ a Health Coach?
clarifying_info.a: Annual costs per Coach: $60K salary plus 20% for other costs (training, benefits, laptop, etc.). There are no other program costs.

exhibits.title: Client's member segmentation by health condition
exhibits.shows: A chart breaking down the client's 5 million members into three segments (Group, Individual, and 65+) and showing the proportion of members in each segment with various health conditions including diabetes, heart disease, and healthy/other. The 65+ segment is noted as Medicare Advantage, premiums funded by government.
exhibits.data: Segment breakdown (% of total members) and disease-condition mix within each segment; 65+ = 20% of members, ~40% of 65+ are diabetic; Individual = ~30% of members; Group = ~50% of members; Group members skew healthier.

exhibits.title: Average cost data (Per Member Per Month)
exhibits.shows: A table listing three member segments with their average PMPM cost and a diabetic cost multiplier applied uniformly across segments.
exhibits.data: Individual: avg PMPM $150, diabetic factor 4x; Group: avg PMPM $100, diabetic factor 4x; 65+: avg PMPM $300, diabetic factor 4x

framework: Program Savings: identify which member segment and disease area generate the highest per-member costs, making the 5% reduction most valuable
Program Costs: calculate total annual cost per Health Coach (salary + other); determine how large a patient portfolio each Coach can manage
Break-even / Profitability: compare annual savings generated by one Coach's portfolio against the annual cost of that Coach
Segment prioritization: assess profitability across all three segments (65+, Individual, Group) and select the most attractive
Risks: test whether key assumptions hold; consider competitive response, regulatory and liability issues

questions.prompt: Which member segment and disease area should the client focus on first, and how many target members are there?
questions.guidance: Strong candidates will identify the 65+ segment as having the highest PMPM costs ($300) and therefore the largest absolute savings potential from a 5% reduction. Within that segment, diabetes is the largest chronic-disease bucket (~40% of 65+ members) and, as a behaviorally driven condition, the most responsive to coaching. Candidates should calculate the number of 65+ diabetics.

math.setup: 65+ share of total members × diabetic share of 65+ segment × total members

questions.prompt: What is the annual cost per Health Coach?
questions.guidance: Candidate must add the 20% overhead to the base salary to arrive at total annual cost.

questions.prompt: How large is each Health Coach's patient portfolio (maximum contacts per month)?
questions.guidance: Candidate should multiply daily contact capacity by working days per month. Monthly contact = once-a-month requirement, so portfolio size = contacts per month.

math.setup: Daily contacts × working days per month
steps: Since each patient is contacted once per month, maximum portfolio = 200 patients

questions.prompt: What are the annual savings generated by one Health Coach managing a portfolio of 65+ diabetics?
questions.guidance: Candidate uses Exhibit 2 to find the average PMPM for 65+ ($300), applies the diabetic cost factor (4x), then the 5% savings rate, and multiplies over 12 months and 200 patients.

math.setup: Avg PMPM for 65+ × diabetic cost factor × 5% savings × 12 months × portfolio size

questions.prompt: Is the Health Coach program profitable for the 65+ diabetic segment? What is the overall profit potential?
questions.guidance: Candidate should compare savings per Coach to cost per Coach, then scale to the full 65+ diabetic population.

math.setup: (Savings per Coach - Cost per Coach) × number of Coaches needed
steps: Number of Coaches needed = 400,000 members ÷ 200 per Coach = 2,000 Coaches
math.answer: $72K profit per Coach; $144MM total annual profit for 65+ diabetic segment

questions.prompt: Is the program profitable for the Individual and Group segments?
questions.guidance: Candidate should apply the same math with the respective PMPM values. Individual ($150 avg PMPM, 4x diabetic factor) yields savings of $60/member/month — same savings rate but half the 65+ savings, making it roughly break-even. Group ($100 avg PMPM, 4x diabetic factor) yields even lower savings, resulting in a loss.

math.setup: Repeat savings calculation with Individual ($150) and Group ($100) PMPM

brainstorming.prompt: There are 650K Group diabetics left uncoached. Is there a way to make the Group segment profitable? Who should the client target if it plans to sell the Health Coach program externally?

categories.name: Improving Group segment economics
ideas: More efficient coaching model (e.g., workplace coaching sessions, bi-monthly contact, group webinars)
Automated or hybrid correspondence to reduce Coach time per member
Target only those Group diabetics predicted to respond with savings well above the 5% average

categories.name: Additional revenue sources for Group segment
ideas: Charge employers a fee for the DM service (employers benefit from reduced absenteeism and lower premiums)
Seek government subsidies or grants for preventive care programs

categories.name: External market expansion — target selection
ideas: Sell Health Coach service to other payers (B2B licensing or SaaS model)
Caution: marketing directly to 65+ diabetics attracts sicker members, increasing total health costs even after savings
Consider pricing model for external sale (per-member, per-outcome, or subscription)
Identify regulatory and data-sharing challenges for external sale

recommendation: Client should launch the Health Coaching program, initially targeting diabetes in the 65+ Medicare segment, where the program generates $72K profit per Coach and $144MM total annual profit — a 2x return on each Coach
The Individual segment is break-even and may be worth including for customer retention and moral/brand rationale
The Group segment is loss-making at current economics and should be deferred unless cost structure or revenue model can be improved
risks: Key assumption: 5% average cost reduction may not hold in practice — a pilot is needed to validate
Portfolio assumption: 8 contacts/day assumes steady-state operations; ramp-up could be slower
Competitive response: as first mover, client may face rapid imitation once program proves out
Regulatory and liability risks: health coaches providing medical advice over phone/email may face licensing and malpractice exposure
Member engagement: reaching patients is difficult; actual portfolio utilization may be below 200
next_steps: Launch a pilot program to validate core assumptions (5% savings, 200-patient portfolio, Coach productivity)
Expand to full 65+ diabetic segment upon pilot success ($144MM annual profit opportunity)
Assess Individual segment inclusion based on pilot results and strategic rationale
Explore Group segment economics through employer partnership models or more efficient delivery
If expanding externally, develop a B2B pricing strategy and address regulatory/data-sharing requirements
